protocol: Unpressurized private-aircraft flight to FL250. The pilot reported starting oxygen by nasal cannula passing FL110 and changing to a rebreather mask passing FL180. Actual oxygen dose and complete cabin pressure history were unavailable.
outcome_window: Initial symptoms approximately 45 minutes into cruise. Later neurological review was at three months. Some deficits reportedly persisted for several years.
locator: Case Report, pp. 200–201 and Discussion p. 201
note: One retrospectively attributed episode. In-flight abdominal and shoulder pain preceded focal and visual symptoms and loss of consciousness during descent. Initial hospital diagnosis was cerebellar ataxia of unknown origin. No hyperbaric therapy was administered.

protocol: Unpressurized private-aircraft flight at 28,000 ft MSL. The pilot reported using supplemental oxygen above 12,000 ft and continued oxygen during descent. Actual oxygen delivery, prebreathe and the complete profile were unavailable.
outcome_window: First symptoms after one hour at cruise. Chamber therapy started approximately 12 hours after landing. Follow-up reported at one year.
note: One author-diagnosed altitude DCS episode. New right arm weakness and paresthesias preceded bilateral symptoms. The patient received an initial compression treatment and seven further treatments, with mild residual right shoulder weakness at the one-year assessment.

protocol: Reported 12 cabin-pressure cycles between 18,000 and 38,000 ft cabin altitude while the aircraft was at FL430. After descent the aircraft flew at FL240 with cabin altitude reported as 8,000 ft. The case narrative says three minutes of cycling, and the introduction describes a ten-minute period.
outcome_window: Symptoms about one hour after the cabin fluctuations. First hyperbaric treatment about 3.5 hours after those fluctuations. Follow-up at one year.
locator: Introduction p. 427 and Case Study pp. 427–428
note: One symptomatic pilot with clinical suspicion favoring neurological DCS. The individual cycles, complete gas history and actual start and end pressures are unavailable. The author abstract and case study do not establish an exposure denominator.
